papers.title: Drift Behavior in a Bounded-Confidence Opinion Model with Media Influence
papers.abstract: People's opinions can change both from their interactions with each other and from their interactions with media sources. Bounded-confidence models (BCMs) of opinion dynamics provide one framework to study such dynamics. In a BCM, the nodes of a network are agents with continuous-valued opinions, and these agents interact with each other via the edges of the network. In this paper, we extend the original Deffuant--Weisbuch (DW) BCM by incorporating influence from two media sources --- one with a positive value and one with a negative value --- to capture the effects of a polarized media landscape. We show both numerically and analytically that our extended DW model exhibits drifting behavior in which a large cluster of opinions shifts toward one of the media agents. We analyze how the drift trajectory and speed depend on the model parameters, and we identify conditions in which drift is promoted or suppressed. Our results provide insight into how competing media sources can influence collective opinion formation in social systems.

papers.title: Adversarial swarms as dynamical systems: a sharp outcome transition at population parity and short predictability horizons
papers.abstract: We study an agent-based model of two adversarial swarms as a dynamical system. Attackers seek a fixed goal while evading defenders; defenders are bound to the goal by a Morse potential and pursue attackers that enter a sphere of influence around it. Agents are self-propelled, interact through Morse and inverse-distance potentials, and are removed on contact, so every encounter ends with a dominant swarm. For 22 population ratios $N_A/N_D$ between 0.05 and 20 (1000 trials each), the probability that the attackers dominate jumps from 0.046 at $N_A/N_D = 1$ to 0.971 at 1.1, and both outcomes occur only for $0.24 \le N_A/N_D \le 1.33$. Without attrition, the center-of-mass motion of both swarms passes the 0-1 test for chaos at every ratio, the goal-bound defenders diverging faster and carrying more entropy. With attrition, twin trajectories differing by a $10^{-8}$ displacement separate to the swarm scale within 0.9 to 1.4 time units, and the displacement changes the winner in about 4% of trials near parity; before contact the attackers damp the perturbation and the defenders amplify it. Over the 22,000-trial ensemble the defenders' largest Lyapunov exponent is positive in 97 to 100% of trials across the contested band, whereas the attackers relax to a regular orbit once it resolves. A finite sensing radius leaves the outcomes far from parity unchanged but produces stand-offs near parity and, at the smaller radius, replaces attrition by fast breaches and stand-offs: the sharp transition is a property of long-range sensing.
